title: What is sensitive data exposure — storing passwords in plain text, sending data over HTTP instead of HTTPS, logging PII — and how to prevent it (hash passwords with bcrypt, enforce HTTPS/TLS, mask sensitive data in logs)?
shortTitle: Sensitive Data Exposure and How to Prevent It

s1_definition.profdef: Sensitive data exposure is the failure to adequately protect confidential data at rest, in transit, and in logs, so it can be read by unauthorized parties. Typical causes are storing passwords in plaintext or with weak hashes, transmitting data over unencrypted HTTP, logging personally identifiable information or secrets, weak or absent encryption of stored data, and leaking data in error messages. The defenses are hashing passwords with a slow algorithm like bcrypt, enforcing TLS/HTTPS everywhere, encrypting sensitive data at rest, masking or tokenizing sensitive fields in logs, and minimizing the data collected and retained.
s1_definition.analogy: Sensitive data exposure is like National Bank of India writing customers' PINs on a public notice board (plaintext storage), shouting account details across the lobby (HTTP instead of HTTPS), and photocopying full card numbers into the daily diary that cleaners can read (PII in logs). The fixes are to store PINs only as scrambled irreversible codes, speak through a private sealed tube (TLS), and in any diary write only the last four digits of a card with the rest blacked out (masking).
s1_definition.oneliner: Protect data at rest, in transit, and in logs — hash passwords, force TLS, and mask sensitive fields.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Sensitive data exposure is the failure to adequately protect confidential data at rest, in transit, and in logs, so it can be read by unauthorized parties. Typical causes are storing passwords in plaintext or with weak hashes, transmitting data over unencrypted HTTP, logging personally identifiable information or secrets, weak or absent encryption of stored data, and leaking data in error messages. The defenses are hashing passwords with a slow algorithm like bcrypt, enforcing TLS/HTTPS everywhere, encrypting sensitive data at rest, masking or tokenizing sensitive fields in logs, and minimizing the data collected and retained.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Sensitive data exposure is like National Bank of India writing customers' PINs on a public notice board (plaintext storage), shouting account details across the lobby (HTTP instead of HTTPS), and photocopying full card numbers into the daily diary that cleaners can read (PII in logs). The fixes are to store PINs only as scrambled irreversible codes, speak through a private sealed tube (TLS), and in any diary write only the last four digits of a card with the rest blacked out (masking).

**One line to remember:** Protect data at rest, in transit, and in logs — hash passwords, force TLS, and mask sensitive fields.

sections.s2_technical:
Passwords must never be stored recoverably. Use a slow, salted hash such as bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2, for example `new BCryptPasswordEncoder(12).encode(raw)`, and verify with `matches(raw, hash)`. These are one-way, so even a database breach does not reveal passwords. Other secrets like API keys live in a secrets manager (Vault, KMS), not in code or config files, and are rotated.

Data in transit must be encrypted with TLS. Enforce HTTPS everywhere, redirect HTTP to HTTPS, use HSTS (`Strict-Transport-Security`) so browsers refuse plain HTTP, and use strong cipher suites. Internal service-to-service traffic should also use TLS, often mutual TLS in a bank. Data at rest — account numbers, PII — should be encrypted with database or application-level encryption, and highly sensitive values like full card numbers are often tokenized so the real value never sits in the main datastore.

Logging is a frequent leak point. Never log passwords, full card numbers, tokens, or raw PII. Mask fields so only the last few characters show, for example logging an account as `****2001`, and redact tokens entirely. For instance a logging filter replaces card patterns before writing. The senior points: classify data so you know what is sensitive, apply the right control per state (hash for passwords, encrypt for recoverable data, mask for logs), return generic error messages that do not leak internal details or data, minimize data collection, and set retention limits. Encryption key management — rotation and separation from the data — is as important as the encryption itself.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India stored passwords in plaintext, and a database backup leaked, exposing every customer's password. This is exactly sensitive data exposure at rest — the fix is irreversible bcrypt hashing so a leak reveals nothing usable.

Problem 2 — A developer logged the full account number and card number on every transfer, and those logs are shipped to a third-party log service readable by many. This is exactly PII exposure in logs — the fix is masking so only the last four digits appear.

Our mini-project builds a `CredentialStore` that hashes passwords, a `SensitiveLogger` that masks account and card numbers, and a `TlsPolicy` helper. The demo shows a password stored as a hash (not recoverable), a masked log line, and a reminder that transport is TLS-only.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's password, an account number, and a card number.

Step 1: `storePassword` produces a salted one-way hash and stores only the hash. The original password is never written anywhere recoverable, so even if the database leaks, attackers get hashes that cannot be reversed to the password.

Step 2: `verify` re-hashes the entered password and compares to the stored hash. A correct password matches without the system ever holding the plaintext. This is the at-rest protection for credentials.

Step 3: `logTransfer` logs the transfer but passes the account and card numbers through `mask`, so only the last four digits appear and the rest is hidden. The log line is useful for support but carries no exposed PII, even if the logs are shipped to a third party.

Step 4: The transport policy confirms HTTPS-only with HSTS, so data in transit is encrypted and browsers refuse plain HTTP. The three states — at rest (hash/encrypt), in transit (TLS), and in logs (mask) — are each protected with the appropriate control.

```text

2026-10-31 23:55:00.011 INFO    [SensitiveDataDemo] Verify correct password: true
```

sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Sensitive data across three states
    │
    ├─ AT REST                 ├─ IN TRANSIT              ├─ IN LOGS
    │  password → bcrypt hash  │  client ─TLS/HTTPS─ API  │  account 123..2001
    │  PAN → tokenize/encrypt  │  service ─mTLS─ service  │   → ****2001 (mask)
    │  (leak = useless)        │  HSTS forces HTTPS       │  token → redacted
    ▼                          ▼                          ▼
  DB breach reveals no secrets  eavesdropper sees ciphertext  logs carry no PII
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Sensitive data exposure is the failure to adequately protect confidential data in its three states — at rest, in transit, and in logs — so that unauthorized parties can read it. The common causes are storing passwords in plaintext or weak hashes, sending data over plain HTTP instead of HTTPS, logging personally identifiable information or secrets, weak encryption of stored data, and leaking data in error messages. In a bank this is especially serious because the exposed data is money, identity, and card details.

My approach is to apply the right control to each state. For passwords and other credentials at rest, I use a slow, salted, one-way hash like bcrypt or Argon2, so even a full database breach yields hashes that cannot be reversed. For recoverable sensitive data like account numbers I use encryption at rest, and for the most sensitive values like full card numbers I use tokenization so the real number never sits in the main datastore. Secrets like API keys live in a vault, not in code, and are rotated.

For data in transit I enforce TLS everywhere, redirect HTTP to HTTPS, enable HSTS so browsers refuse plain HTTP, and use mutual TLS between internal services. For logs, which are a frequent leak point, I mask sensitive fields so only the last four digits of an account or card show and I redact tokens entirely. In my demo the password is stored only as a hash, the transfer log line shows account and card as star-masked last-four values, and the transport policy is HTTPS-only with HSTS.

The nuances I stress are classifying data so I know what is sensitive, minimizing what I collect and setting retention limits, returning generic error messages that do not leak internal details, and treating key management — rotation and separation of keys from data — as being just as important as the encryption itself. Protecting all three states with the appropriate control is what prevents a single mistake from becoming a mass data breach.
